AuthiChain's attestation contract keeps two things separate that a lot of verification systems quietly merge: a decision — verified, warning, blocked — and a status — active, revoked, unknown. A revoked attestation doesn't vanish when it's checked; it stays cryptographically inspectable, so a verifier can show exactly what happened instead of returning a flat no.

The contract also states its own boundary in the interoperability rules rather than leaving it implied: a valid Ed25519 signature (compact JWS, RFC 8032) proves the payload wasn't altered and which key signed it. It does not prove the item in front of you is the one the signature was issued for — a copied QR code or a transferred label still needs a subject-mapping and evidence-continuity check on top of the signature, and the spec says so in plain terms instead of letting "verified" imply more than it does.

That boundary now has adversarial test coverage behind it, not just documentation. This week the suite grew from 7 cases to 13: tampered payloads, wrong signing keys, malformed JWS structure, an unsupported algorithm swapped into the header, malformed GTIN/serial/lot fields, malformed or missing evidence entries, and expiry windows that don't hold up. Warning, blocked, revoked and unknown attestations are all checked to stay readable rather than silently rejected.

Read the contract: https://authichain.com/protocol

reddit.title: Separating "the signature is valid" from "this is the same physical item" in a JWS attestation contract
reddit.body:
I work on AuthiChain, a product-verification platform. We maintain a small versioned attestation contract (v0.1): a signed statement tying a provider-scoped object_id to a physical product identifier (GTIN + serial/lot) as a compact JWS — Ed25519/EdDSA, RFC 8032 — with deterministic JSON canonicalization (recursively sorted keys) before signing.

The part I think is worth discussing here: the interoperability rules explicitly separate what the signature proves from what it doesn't. A valid signature proves payload integrity and issuer-key control. It does not prove the physical item in someone's hand is the subject the signature was issued for — a copied QR code or a relabeled item passes signature verification just fine, so that has to be caught by evidence-continuity and subject-mapping checks outside the crypto, not implied by "verified."

Decision (verified/warning/blocked) and status (active/revoked/unknown) are also kept as separate fields rather than collapsed into one pass/fail — a revoked or blocked attestation stays cryptographically inspectable instead of just erroring out.

This week's change expanded the adversarial test suite behind that contract from 7 cases to 13: tampered payloads, wrong kid, malformed JWS structure, an unsupported alg swapped into the header, malformed GTIN/serial/lot, malformed or missing evidence entries, bad expiry windows, and checks that warning/blocked/revoked/unknown states stay inspectable rather than silently dropped.

Known limitation, stated plainly: Ed25519 offers no protection against a large-scale quantum computer — like all elliptic-curve signatures, it's broken by Shor's algorithm. That's a property of the primitive, not something this contract works around.

Curious what this community would add to the adversarial list for a JWS-based attestation contract like this — what failure mode would you expect us to have missed?

https://authichain.com/protocol

Disclosure: I work on this project.
